metadata.title: Saved Isn't Live.
metadata.subtitle: The Configure Skill (Discord Plugin)
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: once you save a new bot token, is your Discord bot immediately running it? Lands the carry-out that a saved token isn't a live token until a restart, while the access policy takes effect on the very next message.

beats.narration_text: The credential file gets read once, at startup. Save a new token mid-session and you're still running the old one until you restart. So: I saved a new token. It's live now, right?

beats.narration_text: Three modes, one argument slot. No arguments and it shows status — reads both files, tells you whether a token is set, what the access policy is, who's already paired, and hands you one concrete next step. A token as the argument is save mode — trims stray whitespace, creates the channel folder if it's missing, updates the credential file without disturbing anything else already in it, then chmods that file to owner-read-only. The literal word clear is remove mode — deletes the token line, or the whole file if that was all it held. Two files carry all of this. The credential file — token inside — is read exactly once, at session startup. The access file — policy inside — is re-read on every single incoming message. That asymmetry is the design decision: secrets change rarely, so load once and cache; policy changes mid-conversation, so re-read every turn.

The rule is explicit: always push toward an allowlist, never let pairing become permanent. Pairing exists only to capture the Discord IDs you don't know yet, and the moment you have them, the skill offers — without waiting to be asked — to flip the switch itself. That 'without asking' is the design choice: leaving pairing on by default is how you ship a bot anyone can bind to, so the skill takes the initiative for you. One detail is easy to miss. Update the allowlist and it's live on your very next message. Save a new token and nothing changes until you restart — the credential file was loaded once, at startup, and it stays loaded. Skip the restart and you'll think you're running the new token when you're still running the old one.

Here's the gap worth staring at. The skill never checks that what you paste actually looks like a Discord token — no length check, no format check, nothing. Paste a grocery list and it lands in the credential file exactly the same way a real token would. The design bet is that any validator has to guess Discord's token format, and every guess silently rejects legitimate tokens the day Discord tweaks it. So the skill chose no validation over brittle validation. The cost: it trusts you completely at the one moment a fat-fingered paste is most likely to happen.
A saved token isn't a live token — the credential file is only read once, at restart. The access policy has no such wait; it's checked on your very next message.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to understand read-once versus live-reload behavior in credential-based tools. Take a specific tool I use — say a bot with an API token stored in a config file — and walk me through which values are read at startup and cached, which are re-read on every operation, what happens if I update each kind of value mid-session without restarting, and where a tool like this is likely to skip validation and quietly accept a malformed value. Ask me one clarifying question before you answer. Go deeper: ask the same model what a minimally invasive validation layer would look like — one that catches obviously-broken pastes without becoming brittle every time the credential format changes.
